title: US Firm Reflect Orbital Buys Two Skyroot Launches After Vikram-1 Success
excerpt: California-based Reflect Orbital has purchased two dedicated launches from India's Skyroot Aerospace — one on Vikram-1 and one on the in-development Vikram-1U — months after Vikram-1 became India's first privately developed rocket to reach orbit on its maiden flight.
body:
• US company Reflect Orbital has purchased two dedicated launches from India's Skyroot Aerospace to deploy its future spacecraft.
  • The first launch will fly on Vikram-1; the second will use the in-development Vikram-1U, which adds first-stage boosters and improved performance.
  • Financial terms and launch dates were not disclosed in the announcement.
  • The deal follows Vikram-1's successful maiden orbital flight in July 2026 and extends Skyroot's commercial launch manifest across the Vikram family.

Reflect Orbital, a US company building orbital mirrors to redirect sunlight back to Earth, has purchased two dedicated launches from Skyroot Aerospace, the Indian private launch company whose Vikram-1 rocket reached orbit on its first flight in July. The agreement, announced on October 14, 2026, in a release issued via PR Newswire, gives Reflect Orbital assured schedule and capacity, complementing its other planned launches from sites in the United States.

The first launch under the contract will use the Vikram-1 rocket. The second will fly on Skyroot's in-development Vikram-1U, a variant with additional first-stage boosters and improved performance — industry coverage puts the 1U's capacity at about 550 kg to low Earth orbit, against roughly 350 kg for Vikram-1. Neither company disclosed the contract's value or the launch dates.

"There's a real launch capacity shortage right now. We're excited to work with a new launch provider, Skyroot, to help ensure access to space."

— Ben Nowack, Co-Founder and CEO, Reflect Orbital

Sunlight, Delivered From Orbit

Reflect Orbital, based in Hawthorne, California, builds and operates orbital mirrors designed to deliver controlled lighting to precise locations on Earth without ground infrastructure. The company says the redirected sunlight could extend electricity generation at solar farms after sunset, help search-and-rescue teams work at night, and let construction crews operate more safely after dark. Nowack said the company was recently licensed by the Federal Communications Commission to operate its first spacecraft, and that it will keep working with astronomers, local communities and regulators as it scales.

From First Flight to Foreign Customers

Skyroot was founded in Hyderabad in 2018 by former ISRO engineers Pawan Kumar Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka. It became the first Indian private company to launch a rocket into space with the suborbital Vikram-S in 2022. In July 2026, on the mission named Aagman, Vikram-1 became India's first privately developed orbital rocket to achieve orbit on its maiden flight. In May 2026, Skyroot raised nearly $60 million at a $1.1 billion valuation, becoming India's first space-tech unicorn, according to the announcement.

The Reflect Orbital order is an early commercial return on that first flight. For decades, India's launch capability meant ISRO alone; a US customer choosing an Indian private rocket for dedicated missions is a different kind of milestone — overseas buyers entrusting critical payloads to a startup's vehicle. Chandana said Reflect Orbital represents the kind of ambitious global mission the Vikram family is being built to serve, and that the two dedicated launches would give the customer schedule certainty and mission flexibility.

Why the Timing Matters

The deal lands in a tight global launch market. Nowack pointed to a real shortage of launch capacity, and trade coverage of the agreement noted that operators are increasingly buying dedicated vehicles as rideshare slots fill up years in advance. Dedicated launches cost more than a rideshare seat, but they let a customer choose its orbit and timetable — for a company planning a constellation of mirror satellites, that control is the product Skyroot is selling.

What's Next

Skyroot has not announced dates for the two Reflect Orbital missions, and the second depends on the Vikram-1U completing development. Watch for the 1U's first flight and for further foreign orders: each international contract strengthens the case that India's private launch sector, opened up only a few years ago, can compete for the world's small-satellite business rather than only serving domestic customers.
